Megatron Bridge supports transformer layer recomputation, which checkpoints the input of each transformer layer and recomputes the activations for the remaining layers. Megatron Bridge also supports partial transformer layer recomputation, which is beneficial when recomputing a few transformer layers helps to reduce enough GPU memory for the model to fit. results.title: Activation Recomputation — NVIDIA NeMo Framework User Guide
results.content: NeMo supports transformer layer recomputation, which checkpoints the input of each transformer layer and recomputes the activations for the remaining layers. NeMo also supports partial transformer layer recomputation, which is beneficial when recomputing a few transformer layers help to reduce enough GPU memory for model to fit. Transformer layer recomputation is enabled by setting `activations_checkpoint_granularity=full`. The number of transformer layers to recompute can be set using `activations_checkpoint_num_layers` along with `activations_checkpoint_method=block`. If you set `activations_checkpoint_num_layers` as the total number of layers, the inputs of all transformer layers are checkpointed and recomputed. NeMo also supports checkpointing the input to a block of multiple consecutive transformer layers, meaning that a block of transformer layers becomes the recomputation granularity. This recomputation mode can be enabled by setting `activations_checkpoint_method=uniform`, with the number of transformer layers per recomputation block set using `activations_checkpoint_num_layers`. NeMo supports the self-attention recomputation that checkpoints the inputs of each self-attention block and recomputes the intermediate input activations.

Title: Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models
Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models | alphaXiv. Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models. Reducing Activation Recomputation in Large Transformer Models. Researchers from NVIDIA developed sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation to mitigate activation memory bottlenecks and enhance training throughput for large transformer models. These methods achieved approximately 5x reduction in activation memory and a 29-32% improvement in training throughput while reducing recomputation overhead to just 3%. Researchers from NVIDIA developed sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation to mitigate activation memory bottlenecks and enhance training throughput for large transformer models. ### Memory Challenges in Training Large Transformer Models. Training large transformer models has become increasingly challenging due to memory constraints, particularly the memory required to store activations during the backward pass. This paper presents two complementary approaches: sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation, which together enable more efficient training of large transformer models. Memory Challenges in Training Large Transformer Models. Image 4: Memory allocation pattern during training_Figure 9(a): Memory allocation pattern during transformer model training, showing how GPU memory is utilized across different operations._. Mathematically, for a sequence length S, hidden dimension H, and tensor parallel size P, sequence parallelism reduces activation memory from O(S×H) to O(S×H/P) for operations like layer normalization. The second technique, selective activation recomputation, targets specific portions of the transformer architecture that have high memory usage but relatively low computational cost to recompute. The paper provides analytical modeling to estimate activation memory requirements under different parallelism strategies. **Memory Reduction**: The combined approach reduces activation memory by approximately 5x compared to tensor parallelism alone (Figure 1). Image 12: Activation memory reduction_Figure 6: Percentage of full activation memory required by different approaches across model sizes._. By combining sequence parallelism and selective activation recomputation, the authors achieve substantial memory savings and performance improvements that enable training of increasingly large models on existing hardware. The techniques address a critical bottleneck in scaling transformer models to trillions of parameters and demonstrate that thoughtful memory optimization can significantly impact training efficiency. *   This paper introduces Megatron-LM, a transformer model training framework focusing on model parallelism. It provides context on existing work for accelerating training of large transformer models and informs the memory optimization techniques.
